title: Effects of Experimental Sleep Restriction on Energy Intake, Energy Expenditure, and Visceral Obesity

venue.name: Journal of the American College of Cardiology

abstract:
Background

Although the consequences of sleep deficiency for obesity risk are increasingly apparent, experimental evidence is limited and there are no studies on body fat distribution.

Objectives

The purpose of this study was to investigate the effects of experimentally-induced sleep curtailment in the setting of free access to food on energy intake, energy expenditure, and regional body composition.

Methods

Twelve healthy, nonobese individuals (9 males, age range 19 to 39 years) completed a randomized, controlled, crossover, 21-day inpatient study comprising 4 days of acclimation, 14 days of experimental sleep restriction (4 hour sleep opportunity) or control sleep (9 hour sleep opportunity), and a 3-day recovery segment. Repeated measures of energy intake, energy expenditure, body weight, body composition, fat distribution and circulating biomarkers were acquired.

Results

With sleep restriction vs control, participants consumed more calories (P = 0.015), increasing protein (P = 0.050) and fat intake (P = 0.046). Energy expenditure was unchanged (all P > 0.16). Participants gained significantly more weight when exposed to experimental sleep restriction than during control sleep (P = 0.008). While changes in total body fat did not differ between conditions (P = 0.710), total abdominal fat increased only during sleep restriction (P = 0.011), with significant increases evident in both subcutaneous and visceral abdominal fat depots (P = 0.047 and P = 0.042, respectively).

Conclusions

Sleep restriction combined with ad libitum food promotes excess energy intake without varying energy expenditure. Weight gain and particularly central accumulation of fat indicate that sleep loss predisposes to abdominal visceral obesity. (Sleep Restriction and Obesity; NCT01580761).

narrative:
Short impact summary

This experimental sleep-restriction study has become a clear scholarly reference point in sleep and obesity research. It has 124 citations in OpenAlex, places in the top 1% of its field and year, and has also been reused downstream in 127 documented works. The record shows especially strong uptake in review literature, alongside some educational use and limited but real public-facing discussion.

Full narrative

Published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology in 2022, this article examines how experimentally induced sleep curtailment under free access to food affects energy intake, energy expenditure, and regional body composition. Its contribution is notable because the study was framed around a gap in the experimental evidence, particularly the absence of data on body fat distribution. Supported by NIH funding, the work sits at the intersection of sleep medicine, obesity, and cardiometabolic research.

The citation record indicates substantial and sustained academic uptake. OpenAlex reports 124 citations, with citation counts accumulating across successive years after publication, and the work is identified as top 1% most cited for its field and year. Its citing landscape is concentrated in sleep and obesity-related areas, with recurring appearances in venues such as Obesity, Nutrients, Sleep Medicine Reviews, and Diabetes/Metabolism Research and Reviews. The downstream literature is led largely by research articles, but reviews are also prominent, suggesting that the paper is being used both as primary evidence and as a synthesis anchor.

The reuse graph reinforces that role: 127 downstream works are documented, including articles, reviews, book chapters, preprints, and a conference paper. Several recent citing papers continue to situate the study within broader questions about sleep loss, obesity, circadian biology, and metabolic risk, including narrative and systematic reviews that draw on its experimental findings. Scite also shows a small but nontrivial discussion profile, with mostly mentioning statements, one supporting citation statement, and a few contradicting statements, indicating that the paper has entered active scholarly debate rather than being cited only as background.

Beyond the academic literature, the paper shows some teaching-oriented and public science uptake. It is linked in five YouTube videos, including content focused on visceral fat, sleep loss, and metabolic health, which suggests that the study has become a recognizable teaching example for general audiences. Public discourse captured in the available record is limited, but the article was referenced in two podcast episodes associated with Huberman Lab, one of which explicitly discussed the effects of moderate sleep loss on metabolism. Overall, the evidence points to a highly visible and methodologically influential article whose strongest impact is in scholarly synthesis and translational discussion around sleep restriction and obesity.
